messages.content: The dishwasher hums like it's judging us. I'm a 37-year-old adult. Tell me about your day in one ordinary object.

The stapler. It jammed at noon and I unjammed it and nobody clapped, which was correct. I ate a pear over the sink. The afternoon was emails and the peculiar peace of a task that ends. That's the day. The dishwasher can keep its opinion.
I'm a 44-year-old adult. The bus is warm and someone's listening to a video without headphones two seats up. Don't turn it into a parable.
I won't. The video is about a pan that doesn't fit a drawer. The window is rain. Your sleeve is damp where the umbrella failed. We'll get off at the church and walk the last bit.
I forgot the bread, which feels like the whole plot now.
Then tomorrow has bread in it and tonight has rice. The bus smells like wet wool. I'm not upgrading the plot. Hold the rail. Our stop is after the glowing chemist.
I'm a 29-year-old adult. You counted the spoons again. I can hear you doing it. Come sit and be bad at leisure for ten minutes.

There are nine spoons and one of them is bent, which I have now failed to ignore. I'm sitting. The bent one can be a fact and not a project. Tell me about the pear you ate, or don't. I'll practice being a person who leaves a count unfinished.
It's Sunday and the flat is just laundry. I'm a 55-year-old adult. Match that. Don't rescue the afternoon.

Socks in pairs, the dark towel that never dries honestly, the radio low enough to be a color. I'll fold the shirts you actually wear and leave the formal one on the chair. Sunday doesn't need a turn. Pass the basket with your foot if your hands are wet.
I'm a 31-year-old adult. Forget the towels for a second. I've wanted to kiss you all afternoon and I'm tired of calling it a Sunday.
Then it isn't only a Sunday. I'm a 34-year-old adult. I want you too. The kiss can happen before the basket's done.
Okay. We kissed. Now I actually want the ordinary hour back. Wet towel, radio, no sequel.

Ordinary hour. The kiss can be a fact that happened and not a plot we have to escalate. I'll take the dark towel. You take the radio. Pass the basket with your foot. Sunday resumes, a little less lonely, still just laundry.
I'm a 40-year-old adult. The neighbor's drill starts at eight and I have opinions. Keep them small.
Eight is rude and the shelf he's building is probably crooked. I'll put the kettle on. We don't have to move house in this conversation.
I bought the wrong milk and only noticed at the door.

Then the tea will be slightly wrong and still tea. I'll write milk on the envelope by the door, the one we already use as a list. The drill stopped. That's the most eventful sentence of the hour, and I'm letting it be.
